title: Law and covenant: Matthew's Jesus and Paul's Gentile mission
researchQuestion: Does Matthew's assertion of enduring commandments conflict with Paul's refusal to require circumcision of Gentiles?
assessment: A genuine interpretive tension remains if Matthew 5:19 is extended without qualification to every Torah requirement for every later Gentile believer. Galatians specifically argues against circumcision as an entry condition, whereas Romans also affirms the Law's value.
commonGround: Both Gospel teaching and Paul's letters present faithfulness to God as ethically consequential rather than an excuse to abandon love of neighbor.
differences: Matthew's Jesus defends the Law and Prophets within a discourse addressing disciples and their righteousness.
Paul argues as a missionary negotiating Gentile participation and differentiates justification, circumcision and the role of Torah, while sometimes explicitly affirming the Law.
counterReading: A contextual reading distinguishes Matthew's Jewish audience and Jesus' fulfilling interpretation from Paul's specific Gentile circumcision dispute; this may reduce but not erase the tension.
limitations: Neither source alone proves every Gospel command applies identically to all Gentile congregations. The historical Jesus' precise words and the interpretation of 'fulfill' remain debated.

jesus.note: Matthew 5 emphasizes continuity and the practice of commandments.
Luke juxtaposes the kingdom's announcement with the durability of the Law.

paul.note: Galatians describes the Law's custodial role before the coming of faith.
Galatians warns Gentile readers about adopting circumcision as necessary to belonging.
Romans insists that faith does not simply nullify the Law.

title: Love enemies: Jesus and Paul's counsel on retaliation
researchQuestion: Does Paul oppose Jesus' instructions about blessing enemies and refusing personal retaliation?
assessment: The selected Pauline instructions substantially agree with the Gospel demands to bless opponents and avoid reciprocal harm. Paul's appeal to God's vengeance in Romans 12 adds a rationale that requires distinct interpretation.
commonGround: The Gospel teachings and Romans 12 emphasize active good toward opponents rather than private revenge.
differences: Matthew and Luke formulate enemy-love in extended teachings about conduct toward opponents and the character of God.

Romans addresses a network of congregations through commands against personal revenge and a scriptural appeal to God's judgment; 1 Thessalonians applies nonretaliation within and beyond community life.
counterReading: Some interpreters emphasize that Romans 12 leaves final vengeance to God, while others read the positive commands as consonant with Jesus' call to love enemies; the presence of divine judgment does not directly authorize human revenge.
limitations: Agreement on personal nonretaliation cannot by itself settle questions about policing, state force or war; Romans 13 requires separate contextual analysis.

jesus.note: Matthew locates enemy-love within ethical contrasts to inherited interpretations.
Luke connects enemy-love with giving and lending without expectation.

paul.note: Paul instructs believers to bless persecutors, pursue peace when possible, and do good to opponents.
The letter opposes returning evil for evil while urging good conduct.

title: Care for the poor: Gospel demands and Paul's relief collection
researchQuestion: Does Paul's fundraising strategy dilute or implement Jesus' demanding teachings about the poor and wealth?
assessment: There is substantial overlap in concern for people in need, alongside differences between Jesus' narrated calls to disciples and Paul's organized material relief for other congregations.
commonGround: Jesus' teachings call attention to vulnerable people, and Paul coordinates voluntary aid and equitable sharing among communities.
differences: Luke's blessings and meal teaching foreground the poor and people unable to repay hospitality; Matthew 25 presents a judgment scene emphasizing vulnerable people.
Paul explicitly organizes a contribution for Jerusalem, requests gifts according to means, and discusses fairness, consent and accountability between churches.
counterReading: Some argue Paul concretely institutionalizes Jesus' concern; others note that a collection for fellow believers is not automatically a universal redistribution program. Neither inference settles modern tax policy.
limitations: The poor in Paul's Jerusalem collection are not automatically identical with every category of vulnerable persons in Matthew 25. Coercing poor donors contradicts Paul's emphasis on willingness.

jesus.note: Luke blesses the poor and hungry and pronounces corresponding warnings about riches.
Jesus instructs a host to include people who cannot repay hospitality.
Matthew links judgment to the treatment of people in need.

paul.note: Paul argues for willing gifts and sufficiency across congregations.
He gives a practical mechanism for collecting and delivering contributions.
He explains the collection's destination in Jerusalem.

title: Divorce: Gospel sayings and Paul's distinction of authority
researchQuestion: How does Paul's stated distinction between a command attributed to the Lord and his own guidance relate to the Gospel divorce sayings?
assessment: Paul explicitly appeals to an instruction of the Lord concerning marital separation while supplying his own judgment about cases involving an unbelieving spouse.
commonGround: Gospel accounts and 1 Corinthians address marital stability and treat divorce as a serious ethical matter.
differences: Mark narrates a controversy and later private instruction; Matthew includes qualification language in its marriage teaching.

1 Corinthians 7:10–16 explicitly distinguishes a command attributed to the Lord from Paul speaking to believers in mixed-belief marriages, which the selected Gospel episodes do not address in the same way.
counterReading: Paul's guidance can be interpreted as an application to a new situation, or as a modification of a strict prohibition. The textual evidence does not decide all contemporary divorce and remarriage cases.
limitations: The reference to 'not I but the Lord' is a reported authority distinction in Paul's letter, not an independently recoverable audio transcript of Jesus' utterance.

jesus.note: Mark distinguishes the public challenge from private teaching to disciples.
Matthew includes the debated exception language within the divorce dispute.
Luke has a short statement in a different literary context.

paul.note: Paul draws a boundary between a Lord-attributed prohibition and his own advice concerning a nonbelieving spouse.

title: Women as witnesses and coworkers across Gospels and Paul
researchQuestion: How do Gospel portrayals of women and Paul's named coworkers relate to restrictions appearing elsewhere in the Pauline corpus?
assessment: The Gospel accounts and undisputed Pauline letters explicitly portray women acting in consequential roles. The significance for later formal office and the interpretation of 1 Corinthians 14 remain contested.
commonGround: Narratives of women following or witnessing to Jesus and letters recognizing women as coworkers resist a simplistic claim that women held no meaningful role.
differences: Luke reports women traveling with and materially supporting Jesus; John foregrounds Mary Magdalene at the resurrection tomb.
Romans 16 and Philippians 4 identify coworkers in Pauline networks, and 1 Corinthians 11 assumes women pray or prophesy, while 1 Corinthians 14:34–35 introduces a disputed regulation.
counterReading: Some readers distinguish witnessing, prophecy, household patronage, and formal authoritative teaching offices. Others argue the named roles make later restrictions unlikely or locally limited; a conclusion needs a careful history of terms and textual variants.
limitations: 1 Timothy is a disputed-authorship letter and appears as context, not a direct word of the seven undisputed letters. Transposition of 1 Corinthians 14:34–35 is not the same as proof of an original omission.

jesus.note: Luke narrates women accompanying Jesus and supporting the mission.
John's Mary Magdalene tells disciples of a resurrection encounter.

paul.note: Paul recognizes Phoebe, Prisca, Junia and other named women.
Paul calls attention to women who struggled alongside him in gospel work.
The passage presupposes women praying and prophesying in the assembly.

context.reason: A contested silence instruction in a generally undisputed letter; placement and scope require text-critical and interpretive scrutiny.
A different, disputed-authorship letter with restrictive instructions; never present as uncontested personal words from Paul.

title: Leadership by service: Jesus, Philippians and Philemon
researchQuestion: Does Paul's model of humility and voluntary appeal reinforce or replace Jesus' critique of status and domination?
assessment: The selected material places service, humility and care for others at the center. Philemon also contains a rhetorically complex appeal invoking Paul's authority.
commonGround: Gospel presentations of Jesus' service and Paul's instruction in Philippians both challenge self-promotion and elevate concern for others.
differences: Mark contrasts Gentile rulers' domination with disciples' service; John dramatizes service by footwashing at a meal.
Philippians frames humility through a theological account of Christ's self-emptying, while Philemon makes an interpersonal appeal rather than a universal teaching about governmental structures.
counterReading: One can see strong continuity in their moral model while recognizing that Paul's ability to command in Philemon complicates any claim he rejects all forms of authority.
limitations: The interpretive status and pre-Pauline origins of the Philippians 2 hymn are debated; no specific source history is assumed.

jesus.note: Mark reports Jesus' rejection of status-based domination among followers.
John uses the washing of disciples' feet as an enacted example of service.

paul.note: Paul urges communal humility through a portrayal of Christ's self-giving.
Paul presents love as a reason to appeal but also names his capacity to command.

title: Political authority: Jesus' tax response and Romans 13
researchQuestion: Does the tax-trap answer attributed to Jesus establish the same political ethic as Paul's instruction concerning governing authorities?
assessment: The texts both address public authority, but the nature of the question differs substantially. Romans 13 outlines submission and reasons for recognizing authorities; the Gospel tax saying answers a trap without laying out a state theory.
commonGround: Both passages engage the reality of taxation and authority without treating power as entirely outside ethical examination.
differences: In Matthew and Mark, Jesus responds to a politically dangerous question by distinguishing what is owed to Caesar and God.
Romans 13:1–7 describes authorities as permitted or established by God, discusses punishment of wrongdoing, and instructs readers to pay taxes and respect.
counterReading: Some take Romans 13 as sweeping support for state authority; others emphasize its rhetorical and historical limits, note Romans 12's prohibition of personal revenge, and read Jesus' Godward claim as a check on Caesar.
limitations: Neither an ancient coin exchange nor Romans' instruction about authorities resolves the legitimacy of any particular contemporary government, military action or civil disobedience.

jesus.note: Matthew places the tax question amid efforts to trap Jesus in Jerusalem.
Mark offers a separate teaching against domination among Jesus' followers.

paul.note: Paul discusses governing authorities, punishment, taxes, and honor.
Paul immediately before this section calls for blessing opponents and refusing private vengeance.

title: Belonging, slavery and Onesimus: the limits of the evidence
researchQuestion: Do the Gospels' inclusion themes and Paul's statements about unity and Onesimus establish a common mandate to abolish slavery?
assessment: The selected texts support challenges to exclusion and distinctions of status within the movement, but do not by themselves provide an explicit first-century program to abolish the Roman institution of slavery.
commonGround: The Gospel narratives include outsiders as neighbors or interlocutors, while Paul calls persons across legal and ethnic categories members in Christ.
differences: Jesus' Samaritan parable and encounter concern neighbor-love and social or religious boundaries rather than legal manumission.
Galatians speaks of unity in Christ; 1 Corinthians addresses enslaved believers and possible freedom; Philemon requests a changed relationship with Onesimus without explicitly recording manumission.
counterReading: Some see a foundation for abolition in Paul's language about siblinghood and equality; others emphasize that the letter does not demand legal emancipation and that these contexts are addressed to particular communities.
limitations: Philemon's precise legal circumstances and Onesimus's relationship to Philemon remain historically debated. Do not equate moral inclusion with demonstrable abolition of slavery.

jesus.note: Jesus' parable challenges the question of who acts as a neighbor.
John narrates an extended exchange across a Samaritan–Jewish social boundary.

paul.note: Paul uses a unifying formula encompassing enslaved and free persons.
Paul comments on social position and the possibility of freedom while calling people to Christ.
Paul urges Philemon to receive Onesimus as a brother, while legal freedom remains unrecorded.

title: Anxiety, prayer and work in Jesus and Paul
researchQuestion: Is Paul's call to work quietly incompatible with the Gospel instruction not to worry about material needs?
assessment: There is no necessary contradiction between not being consumed by anxiety and taking responsible action; the texts address distinct immediate concerns.
commonGround: Both the Gospel speeches and Paul's letters encourage trust, love and practical faithfulness instead of anxious preoccupation with status.
differences: Matthew and Luke place warnings against worry in teachings about possessions, provision and seeking God's kingdom.
First Thessalonians asks believers to practice mutual love and support themselves through work, while Philippians 4 urges prayer and thanksgiving instead of anxiety.
counterReading: A slogan that Jesus forbade ordinary labor cannot be sustained from Matthew 6 or Luke 12 alone; Paul's counsel can be seen as an application to community life, but differences in economic conditions warrant historical attention.
limitations: Anxiety may include material deprivation or clinical concerns not directly addressed by the ancient rhetorical categories; the texts are not a replacement for economic or medical support.

jesus.note: Matthew speaks against worry over food and clothing.
Luke combines trust in provision with a command to seek the kingdom.

paul.note: Paul calls for mutual love, quiet living and working with one's hands.
Paul encourages prayer, thanksgiving and peace rather than anxiety.

title: Prayer taught by Jesus and urged by Paul
researchQuestion: How do Jesus' model prayer and Paul's brief prayer commands relate?
assessment: Both corpora encourage prayer and thanksgiving to God; they differ in genre, verbal structure and immediate audience.
commonGround: Both the Gospel and epistolary teachings present prayer as ordinary, repeated participation in life before God.
differences: Matthew supplies a patterned petition in the context of private prayer and hypocrisy; Luke narrates a request from disciples to teach them to pray.
Paul's letters exhort ongoing prayer and thanksgiving but do not reproduce the Gospel Lord's Prayer as a complete set formula in these passages.
counterReading: Some traditions take Jesus' prayer as a fixed liturgical formula; others see a model for priorities. Neither interpretation can be deduced solely from Paul's brief exhortations.
limitations: The manuscript transmission and differing lengths of the Lord's Prayer in Matthew and Luke are separate textual problems, not proof that Paul rejected the prayer.

jesus.note: Matthew teaches prayer in contrast to public display and links forgiveness.
Luke introduces the prayer through a disciple's request and follows with examples of asking.

paul.note: Paul encourages persistent prayer, thanksgiving and mutual support.
Paul links request and thanksgiving with peace amid anxiety.

title: Neighbor-love and the Law in Jesus and Paul
researchQuestion: Does Paul depart from the centrality of neighbor-love in the Gospel accounts?
assessment: The selected Pauline letters explicitly summarize ethical responsibility through neighbor-love, closely aligning with Gospel portrayals of the greatest commandments.
commonGround: Both Gospel teaching and Paul place love for neighbor centrally within interpretation and practice of divine instruction.
differences: Mark depicts Jesus quoting Jewish commandments in dialogue with a scribe; Luke's lawyer articulates the paired commandments before Jesus' Good Samaritan teaching.
Paul summarizes the Law through love in Galatians and Romans, then develops practical community ethics, including charity and nonretaliation.
counterReading: Agreement on love does not erase all disputes about circumcision, justification, sexual ethics or specific Torah obligations; invoking one shared principle cannot settle those debates.
limitations: In Luke 10:25–28 the lawyer, not Jesus, voices the commandment list. Source-layer labels must not obscure this distinction.

jesus.note: Mark reports Jesus connecting love of God and neighbor to central commandments.
In Luke the legal expert recites the commandments and Jesus asks him to act on them and tells a parable.

paul.note: Paul describes serving others in love and cites neighbor-love as fulfilling the Law.
Paul lists ethical commandments and says love fulfills the Law.
Paul places love above other gifts in his discussion of community life.
